bib.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Chapter 7: Model Assessment and Selection

question: How should the generalization error of a learned model be estimated and used to choose among models?
contributions: Decomposes test error into irreducible error, bias and variance and shows it behaves differently for 0-1 loss
Derives optimism of training error and in-sample error estimates (Cp, AIC, BIC, MDL, VC/SRM)
Presents CV and bootstrap (.632, .632+) as direct estimates of extra-sample error and compares them in simulation
Shows the wrong and right way to do CV with feature screening
Shows CV estimates expected error Err, not the conditional ErrT

limits: Simulations are small (N=20 to 80, 100 or 50 replications) and use only kNN, best-subset linear models and stumps; AIC/BIC/SRM compared on four scenarios only.
SRM result depends on constants a1,a2; authors chose the most favourable; Cherkassky and Ma (2003) disputed their application of SRM.
AIC formula does not strictly hold for 0-1 loss; VC dimension is hard to compute and bounds are loose.
No estimator estimates the conditional error ErrT well from a single training set.
CV and bootstrap can underestimate error by about 10% for trees; a separate test set is then needed.
Predates modern large-data deep learning practice; assumes iid data (no grouped, temporal or distribution-shift splits).
practices: With ample data, split into train, validation and test sets (typically 50/25/25) and keep the test set in a vault until the end (Sec 7.2, p222).
Do not reuse the test set to pick models; it then underestimates the true error (Sec 7.2, p222).
Use 5- or 10-fold cross-validation as a compromise between bias and variance (Sec 7.10.1, p243).
Apply CV to the whole modelling pipeline: leave samples out before any supervised selection or filtering; unsupervised screening may be done before (Sec 7.10.2, p246).
Report the standard error of the CV estimate, and consider the one-standard-error rule for a parsimonious model (Sec 7.10.1, p244; 7.10.3, p249).
Use AIC/BIC only for models linear in parameters or with an estimable effective number of parameters; for adaptive nonlinear models such as trees use CV or bootstrap (Sec 7.11.1, p253).
Use the .632+ bootstrap rather than .632 when the fit overfits heavily (Sec 7.11, p252).
Choose tuning parameters from an estimate of prediction error for the actual loss, since the best parameter differs between squared error and 0-1 loss (Sec 7.3.1, p228).
Only compare models by relative error: a constant bias in an estimate does not change which model is selected (Sec 7.11.1, p253).
